explanations.explanation: Julius is a centurion, a Roman officer, and he belongs to the Imperial Regiment. Paul and the other prisoners are handed over to him (Acts 27:1). From here on, he's the one watching over them. Paul just got a new boss, friend.

Cornelius is a centurion too, but he's in a different story, in Caesarea (Acts 10:1). Easy to mix up, since centurions come in bunches. The man holding Paul here is Julius, from the Imperial Regiment (Acts 27:1).

Festus is the governor who told Paul, "You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!" (Acts 25:12). So he's part of how Paul ended up on this trip. But the text says the prisoners are handed over to a centurion named Julius (Acts 27:1). I think a governor has better things to do than ride along on a boat.

True. At Sidon, Julius "treated Paul with consideration, allowing him to visit his friends and receive their care" (Acts 27:3). Paul is still a prisoner, but a friendly stop is a friendly stop. Say what you want about a long trip, a visit with friends makes it better.

This one is actually true. The text says Julius "treated Paul with consideration, allowing him to visit his friends and receive their care" (Acts 27:3). So Paul doesn't just sit on the ship at Sidon. He gets to see his friends, and they get to care for him.

The winds. They sail to the lee of Cyprus "because the winds were against us" (Acts 27:4). The lee is the side that blocks the wind, so the island helps shield them. Sailing is a lot like rolling dough: when it pushes back, you work around it.
No pirates in this verse, friend. The text says they sail to the lee of Cyprus "because the winds were against us" (Acts 27:4). The danger here is the weather, not anybody climbing aboard.

Currents sound like a smart guess for the sea. But the text names the winds: "because the winds were against us" (Acts 27:4). The lee of Cyprus is the side sheltered from them. Sometimes the answer is just the weather.

Alexandria. Julius finds an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and puts them on board (Acts 27:6). That's the ship that finally goes where they're headed. A boat going your direction is worth finding, friend.
Tyre isn't named in this passage. The text says Julius finds an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy (Acts 27:6). So the ship comes from Alexandria.
Joppa doesn't show up here at all. The ship Julius finds at Myra is an Alexandrian ship, sailing for Italy (Acts 27:6). The name is the whole clue: Alexandrian means from Alexandria.
Not quite. The text says "we had moved along the coast with difficulty" before they reached Fair Havens (Acts 27:8). The sailing is still hard along Crete. Easy sailing hasn't shown up yet, friend.

False is right. They move along the coast of Crete "with difficulty" before they come to Fair Havens (Acts 27:8). The wind has already been against them earlier on this trip. So Crete is no free ride, friend.

explanations.answer: Disaster and great loss even of their lives
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says, "Men, I can see that our voyage will be filled with disaster and great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well" (Acts 27:10). That's a serious warning, and he gives it plainly. He names the ship, the cargo and the people on board.

explanations.answer: A long delay but no real danger
explanations.explanation: Paul says a lot more than a delay. He says the voyage "will be filled with disaster and great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well" (Acts 27:10). Danger is exactly what he's pointing at.

explanations.answer: A sickness spreading among the prisoners
explanations.explanation: Sickness never comes up. Paul warns of "disaster and great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well" (Acts 27:10). His warning is about the voyage itself, and it covers the ship, the cargo and the lives on board.

The text says the opposite. "Contrary to Paul's advice, the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship" (Acts 27:11). So Julius doesn't go along with Paul. He goes with the other two voices.

False is right. "Contrary to Paul's advice, the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship" (Acts 27:11). Julius hears Paul, but he follows the other two. I'd be a little nervous right about here, friend.

The pilot. The centurion "was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship" (Acts 27:11). The pilot steers the ship, so you can see why his word carries weight. But Paul's advice is the one the text says Julius went against.
The soldiers aren't mentioned in this verse. The text says Julius "was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship" (Acts 27:11). The two voices that win him over are the pilot and the owner.

The prisoners are the ones in line to be guarded, not the ones Julius listens to. The text says he "was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship" (Acts 27:11). Paul himself is a prisoner, and the text says Julius went against his advice.

explanations.answer: The harbor isn't good for spending winter
explanations.explanation: Right. "The harbor was unsuitable to winter in," so the majority decided to sail on (Acts 27:12). They're hoping to reach Phoenix, another harbor on Crete. It's a plan with a reason, even if it's the one that went against Paul.

explanations.answer: The town of Lasea won't let them stay
explanations.explanation: Lasea is only named as the town near Fair Havens (Acts 27:8). The text never says it turns them away. The reason is the harbor: it "was unsuitable to winter in" (Acts 27:12).

explanations.answer: Paul tells them the weather will hold
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite. He warns that the voyage "will be filled with disaster and great loss" (Acts 27:10). The majority sails on because the harbor was unsuitable to winter in (Acts 27:12). Paul is not the one telling them to go.
That's the one. "A cyclone called the Northeaster swept down across the island" (Acts 27:14). The gentle wind didn't last long. One verse it's calm, and the next verse it's a cyclone.

explanations.answer: A hailstorm like the one in Egypt
explanations.explanation: The hail in Egypt is its own story (Exodus 9:23). Here the text names a cyclone called the Northeaster that "swept down across the island" (Acts 27:14). Different storm, friend.

explanations.answer: A whirlwind out of the desert
explanations.explanation: No desert in this verse, friend. This storm is at sea, and the text calls it a cyclone called the Northeaster (Acts 27:14). It sweeps down across the island of Crete.
The text says it was close. Passing Cauda, "we barely managed to secure the lifeboat" (Acts 27:16). Barely is not no trouble at all. I think those sailors were holding on with everything they had.
False is right. As they pass Cauda, the text says "we barely managed to secure the lifeboat" (Acts 27:16). That's a tough job in a storm. They get it done, but only just.

explanations.answer: They pass ropes under the ship
explanations.explanation: Yes. The crew "used ropes to undergird the ship" (Acts 27:17). That means they wrapped ropes around it to hold it together. A ship in a storm needs all the help it can get.

explanations.answer: They nail extra boards on the ship
explanations.explanation: Boards and nails aren't in the text. The crew "used ropes to undergird the ship" (Acts 27:17). That means ropes passed under the ship, not extra boards.

explanations.answer: They tie the ship to the lifeboat
explanations.explanation: The lifeboat was just hoisted up on board (Acts 27:17), so it's not out there to tie to. What the crew does next is use ropes to undergird the ship. They pass the ropes under it.

True. "On the third day, they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands" (Acts 27:19). The day before, they'd begun tossing the cargo (Acts 27:18). Now they're throwing gear over too. When you start tossing the ship's own equipment, the storm has your full attention.

This one is actually true. The text says "on the third day, they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands" (Acts 27:19). They did it themselves, and it came right after the cargo went over.

explanations.answer: They lose all hope of being saved
explanations.explanation: That's the text. "We abandoned all hope of being saved" (Acts 27:20). No sun, no stars, and the storm still battering them. It's a heavy moment, so I won't joke about it.

explanations.answer: They hope another ship will find them
explanations.explanation: The text gives no other ship. It says "we abandoned all hope of being saved" (Acts 27:20). Hope is gone, and that's the whole picture.

explanations.answer: They hope Julius will find a way
explanations.explanation: Julius doesn't come up in this verse. The text says "we abandoned all hope of being saved" (Acts 27:20). After many days of no sun and no stars, hope is gone.

explanations.answer: They should have taken his advice and stayed
explanations.explanation: Right. Paul says, "Men, you should have followed my advice not to sail from Crete. Then you would have averted this disaster and loss" (Acts 27:21). He puts that out there first. Then he moves on to what comes next.

explanations.answer: They should have waited for a better wind
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say anything about a better wind. He says, "you should have followed my advice not to sail from Crete" (Acts 27:21). His point is about his own advice and not sailing.

explanations.answer: They should have found a bigger ship there
explanations.explanation: A bigger ship isn't in his words. Paul says, "you should have followed my advice not to sail from Crete. Then you would have averted this disaster and loss" (Acts 27:21). Bigger wouldn't fix it, friend. He's talking about not sailing at all.
True. Paul says, "you will not experience any loss of life, but only of the ship" (Acts 27:22). Think about how that lands after days of no hope. That's why he says to keep up their courage.
This one is true. Paul says, "you will not experience any loss of life, but only of the ship" (Acts 27:22). Not one life is lost, according to him. The loss he names is the ship.

The ship. Paul says there will be no loss of life, "but only of the ship" (Acts 27:22). The cargo and tackle are already going over the side (Acts 27:18-19). The people are what matter, and Paul says they'll be fine.
The lifeboat was just hoisted aboard earlier (Acts 27:17), and Paul doesn't single it out. He says there will be no loss of life, "but only of the ship" (Acts 27:22). The loss he names is the ship.
A mast isn't in Paul's words. He says "you will not experience any loss of life, but only of the ship" (Acts 27:22). The whole ship, friend, not one piece of it.
Yes. The angel says, "Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar" (Acts 27:24). That's the same Caesar Paul appealed to (Acts 25:12). So Paul has somewhere to be, storm or no storm.
Jerusalem isn't in the angel's words. The angel says, "you must stand before Caesar" (Acts 27:24). That's where Paul is headed.
Sidon was back at the start, where Julius let Paul visit his friends (Acts 27:3). The angel's message is about what's ahead. He says, "you must stand before Caesar" (Acts 27:24).
Paul says the opposite. "However, we must run aground on some island" (Acts 27:26). Everyone's lives are safe, but the ship isn't sailing into port. Paul tells them about both parts.

False is right. Paul says, "However, we must run aground on some island" (Acts 27:26). That fits with what he said earlier, that the loss would be the ship (Acts 27:22). Safe lives, a lost ship, and a lot of story still ahead.
